We have already learnt that different kinds of materials are produced
out of various metabolic activities.
Some of these may be harmful for the
organism are removed from their body or packed and stored in some other
forms.
These are all wastes produced in the body of an organism.
We have already discussed how organisms get rid of gaseous wastes
generated during photosynthesis or respiration.
Other metabolic activities
generate nitrogenous wastes that have to be removed along with salts,
excess water and several other materials.
Excretion is the term coined for
all the biological process involved in separation and removal of wastes or
non useful products from the body. (In latin ex means 'out', crenere means
'shift'.)
Now let us study how excretion takes place in human beings.
4.1 Excretion in Human Beings
A number of reactions take place during various metabolic activities.
Many useful substances and energy are produced.
At the same time many
other things happen such as, toxic wastes may be produced, water content
may increase, ionic balance (homeostasis) in the body may be disturbed.
The waste products include carbon dioxide, water, nitrogenous compounds
like ammonia, urea, uric acid, bile pigments, excess salts etc.
The most
poisonous of all waste products of metabolism is ammonia.

4.3.2 Urinary bladder
It is a median, pear shaped and distensible sac.
It is situated in the
pelvic region on the ventral side of the rectum in the abdomen.
It stores
300-800ml of urine temporarily which is brought by two ureters.
4.3.3 Urethra
It is a tube that takes urine from urinary bladder to outside.
The opening
of urinary bladder into urethra is guarded by a ring of muscles or sphincter.
Urethra is 4 cm long in females and open in to vestibule where as in males
it is about 20cm long.
Its opening is separate in females but is in common
with the reproductive tract in males (urino-genital duct).
4.4 Micturition
The urine is temporarily stored in the bladder.
There are two sets of
circular sphincter muscles in the bladder.
When the bladder is filling up,
both these sets of muscles are constricted, so the exit is closed.
However
as the pressure of the urine increases the walls of the bladder are stretched
and this triggers off an automatic reflex action which causes the upper
sphincter to relax.
But the lower sphincter is under the control of brain.
So urination is controlled.
Control of urination is not possessed by very
young children but is gradually learned.
Urinary bladder can store a maximum of 700-800 ml. of urine.
Urge
for micturition occurs when urinary bladder is filled with 300 - 400 ml. of
urine.
The stretched bladder stimulates nerve endings and sends signlas to
the brain.
At this time the urge becomes painful and leads to voluntary
micturition (release of urine from urinary bladder).
Total amount of urine
excreted per day is about 1.6-1.8 litres.
Its quantity increases with larger
intake of fluids like water, fruit juices and decreases with lesser intake.

4.5 Composition of urine
Urine is light yellowish fluid.
Urochrome formed by the breakdown
of haemoglobin in the blood is responsible for the yellowish colour of
urine.
It is a transparent fluid formed by urinary system.
Composition of
normal urine varies considerably depending on several factors.
For instance
taking a protein rich diet will results the formation of more urea in the
urine.
This is because the proteins get de-aminated in the liver with
subsequent formation of urea.
Even sugar can appear in a normal person
after a heavy intake of carbohydrates (sugars).
A large intake of liquids or
water - rich food increases the volume of water in the blood, hence more
often urine is excreted.
Urine contains 96% of water, 2.5% of organic substances (urea, uric
acid, creatine, creatinine, water soluble vitamins, hormones, and oxalates
etc) and 1.5% of inorganic solutes (sodium, chloride, phosphate, sulphate,
magnesium, calcium, iodine etc).
It is acidic (pH=6.0)in the beginning
but gradually becomes alkaline due to breakdown of urea to form ammonia.

4.9 Excretion in other organisms
Different organisms use varied strategies in excretion.
Specific
excretory organs are absent in unicellular organisms.
These organisms
remove waste products by simple diffusion from the body surface into the
surrounding water.
Fresh water organisms like Amoeba, Paramoecium
possess osmoregulatory organelle called contractile vacuole.
It collects
excess water and waste from the cell and slowly moves in the cytoplasm,
reaches the surface and bursts to release its content to outside.
The main
excretion takes place through body surface (Diffusion).
Multicellular organisms possess different excretory organs for
removal of waste materials from the body.
Structural and functional
complexity of excretory organs increases from sponges to humans.

Do plants excrete like animals ?
We are amazed to answer such type of questions.
You are aware that a
variety of end products are formed during metabolism and these

Plants does not have specific organs to
excrete these wastes.
Plants break down the waste substances at much
slower rate than the animals.
Hence the production and accumulation of
waste is also much slower in plants.
Green plants in darkness (in night

water as respiratory waste products.
Oxygen is generated during
photosynthesis as a product, that exits out side through stomata of leaves
and lenticels of stem.

Plants can get rid of excess water by a process like transpiration and

Waste products may be stored in leaves, bark, and fruits.

parsed_output.answer:
Excretion is the process by which living organisms remove waste products and excess substances from their bodies. These wastes are generated as a result of various metabolic activities, such as respiration, digestion, and other cellular processes. The waste products include substances like carbon dioxide, water, nitrogenous compounds (like ammonia, urea, and uric acid), and excess salts. These substances can be harmful if not removed, so excretion is essential for maintaining the balance of the body's internal environment.

The process of urine formation involves several steps. First, the kidneys filter the blood through tiny structures called nephrons. In the glomerulus of the nephron, blood is filtered, and water, salts, and waste products are separated from the blood. This initial filtrate then passes through the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), where useful substances like glucose, amino acids, and some ions are reabsorbed back into the blood. Next, in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and the loop of Henle, further reabsorption and secretion of ions occur. Finally, the remaining fluid, now called urine, is concentrated through the collecting duct and stored in the urinary bladder until it is excreted through the urethra.
